title: Paraṃ mṛtyo: go by your own road
theme: Death is asked to take its own road, not the path of the gods, and is told plainly not to harm the speakers’ children and people.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: the path that is «पूर्वोक्तमार्गद्वयादन्यम्», other than the two paths just named
The anonymous commentator: «पन्थां पन्थानमन्वनुसृत्य परेहि गच्छ» — following that path, go
A Vedic accusative beside the classical panthānam, which is how the commentator glosses it.
The anonymous commentator: «तव स्वः स्वभूतः पन्था अस्ति» — the path that is your own

words.meaning: than the path of the gods
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «देवयानादर्चिरादिमार्गात्पितृयाणमार्गाञ्च» — than the path of the gods, the path of light, and than the path of the fathers
The anonymous commentator: «चक्षुष्मते शृण्वते श्रोत्रवते ते तुभ्यं» — to you, who have eyes and ears

words.role: main verb of the second line

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «प्रजां मा रीरिषो मा हिंसय» — do not harm our offspring

words.gram: verb, reduplicated aorist 2nd sg. (injunctive, with mā)

words.context: The anonymous commentator: he takes them as dependants: «वीरान्भृत्यानपि मा रीरिषः»

sandhi.type: -aḥ before a vowel other than a; -aḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: svaḥ + itaraḥ → sva itaraḥ, the visarga dropped (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)); itaraḥ + devayānāt → itaro devayānāt (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)).
rīriṣaḥ + mā → rīriṣo mā (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)); mā + uta → mota (P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः)).

sandhi_exceptions.note: mṛtyo · anu: the o of the vocative kept before a without elision (classical mṛtyo ’nu); a Vedic hiatus (prakṛtibhāva, P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्यान्तःपादमव्यपरे)), printed so in every witness.

samasa.meaning: the path by which the gods go

morphology.note: The a-stem sva ‘own’, not svar ‘heaven’; so the visarga drops before itaraḥ (sva itaraḥ) instead of becoming r. The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text omits the word (corrections.json, a witness error); the commentator reads it («स्वः स्वभूतः»).
A reduplicated aorist of √riṣ, used with mā as a prohibition (injunctive).

translation.literal: O Death, go away along the further path, which is your own, other than the path of the gods. To you who have eyes, who hear, I speak: do not harm our offspring, nor our men.
translation.readable: Death, go away by your own road, the far road that is not the path of the gods. You see and you hear, so I say this to you: do not harm our children, and do not harm our people.

anvaya: मृत्यो यः ते स्वः देवयानात् इतरः [पन्थाः] [तम्] परम् पन्थाम् अनु परेहि । चक्षुष्मते शृण्वते ते ब्रवीमि । नः प्रजाम् मा रीरिषः उत वीरान् मा [रीरिषः] ।
syntax: A command (anu parehi) with its object panthām, defined by a relative clause (yas te sva itaro devayānāt); then a statement (bravīmi) addressed to Death, described by two datives; then two prohibitions with mā and the aorist rīriṣaḥ, the second sharing the verb.

ambiguities.note: The verse contrasts Death’s road only with the path of the gods. The commentator adds the path of the fathers: Death is to keep away from both, the two roads the dead may take.
Literally ‘heroes, men’; the commentator explains them as dependants (bhṛtyān).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: One triṣṭubh verse printed in two lines; the checker counts 21 and 22 syllables (the first line is short by one, mṛtyo anu being kept in hiatus but counted as written).

beginner: Here the speaker talks to Death directly. Go away, it says, by your own road, the far one that is not the path of the gods. The old commentator explains that in Vedic thought the dead may travel by two paths, the path of the gods and the path of the fathers; Death is asked to keep off both and go its own way. Then the speaker adds: you have eyes and you hear, so listen to me. The commentator imagines Death objecting that it cannot see or hear a prayer, and the verse answering that it can. The request that follows is simple and human: do not harm our children, and do not harm our people. The same verse opens a funeral hymn of the Ṛgveda.
analogy: Like asking a stranger walking towards your house to keep to the road and pass by.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That Death go by its own road, other than the path of the gods, and harm neither the speakers’ offspring nor their people.

commentary.q: Why say that Death has eyes and ears?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator imagines Death saying it is blind and deaf, and so cannot see or hear the one who prays; the verse answers that Death does see and hear: «चक्षुष्मते शृण्वते श्रोत्रवते ते तुभ्यं».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the path of the gods is the path of light (arcirādi-mārga), and with it the path of the fathers; Death’s own road is other than both, and the speaker says, in effect, I shall go by one of these two, I do not look to you («अहं त्वेताभ्यामन्यतरेण वा गमिष्यामि न त्वामीक्षे»).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this verse is in the edition’s sources. Only the anonymous commentator comments on it, and his reading is a prayer to the Lord (paramātman) without a school argument; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s files contain no comment on this verse, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The verse does not plead or bargain; it tells a feared power what not to do, in a few words. Speaking plainly to what we fear, rather than avoiding it, is a kind of courage. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Who are the people you would most want to protect?
reflect.deeper: Why might the verse insist that Death sees and hears?
reflect.practice: Say aloud, once, a fear you usually keep silent, and notice what changes.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentator comments on this anuvāka; the edition’s Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara files have no comment on it (the concordance maps are empty here, correctly).
The same verse is Ṛgveda 10.18.1, the first verse of a funeral hymn. The edition imports Ṛgveda passages only from maṇḍala 1, so its wording is not checked here.

A footnote of the Ānandāśrama editor, printed in the edition’s anonymous-commentary file at the end of 10.47 but keyed by a + mark to this verse, says that the mantra also stands in Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 6.7, where Sāyaṇa explains its first half differently: go by that other path, the one that is your own. The note is the editor’s, not the anonymous commentator’s.

flags.note: The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text omits स्व (corrections.json, a witness error); the base, the Tirupati e-text and the commentary read it.
The Ānandāśrama editor’s footnote on this verse (Sāyaṇa on TA 6.7) is filed under 10.47 in the anonymous-commentary file; it is paraphrased under references, not quoted.
